meta.title: Who really said "The mind is everything. What you think you become"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Neither the Buddha nor Gandhi. It is not in the Pali canon, and the earliest documented English instance is reported in Ralph Waldo Trine's New Thought bestseller In Tune with the Infinite (1897). The Dhammapada says something related — and pointedly different.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The mind is everything. What you think you become'?
meta.ogDescription: A quote with two famous owners and no source. Not in the Pali canon; not in Gandhi's writings in this form. The earliest documented instance is an 1897 American self-help book.

answer.label: Neither the Buddha nor Gandhi — a modern maxim
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · earliest documented English instance reported 1897
answer.sourceLine: This line has the unusual distinction of two famous owners and no source. It is not in the Pali canon — not the Dhammapada, not the Nikayas. It is also not Gandhi in this wording, though a close cousin of it genuinely circulates under his name. The earliest documented English instance is reported in Ralph Waldo Trine’s In Tune with the Infinite (1897), a New Thought bestseller that later fed straight into Think and Grow Rich and the whole positive-thinking industry. That lineage matters: this is a law-of-attraction sentence wearing a monk’s robe.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Majjhima Nikaya 19, on what the mind keeps pursuing
Reported in R. W. Trine, In Tune with the Infinite (1897)

source.excerpt: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.
trail: The Pali test comes first and it is decisive: the sentence appears in no canonical Buddhist text. What people are half-remembering is Dhammapada verses 1 and 2, the Twin-Verses, quoted above in Max Müller’s 1881 translation read them free ↗.

Read them side by side and the difference is not cosmetic. The Dhammapada is making a claim about karma — that acting from a corrupted or a pure mind brings suffering or happiness after it, like a wheel or a shadow. ‘What you think you become’ is a claim about self-creation, which is a different, and much more modern, idea. Majjhima Nikaya 19 is the other near-miss: whatever a monk keeps pursuing in thought becomes the inclination of his awareness. That is a point about habit, not manifestation.

For the English wording, the earliest documented instance we could find reported is Ralph Waldo Trine’s In Tune with the Infinite (1897). One honest caveat: we take that from Bodhipaksa’s trace rather than from the printed 1897 page, and he notes he could not establish where Trine got it either — so treat 1897 as the earliest documented instance, not a proven coinage the trace ↗.
source.excerptNote: The verse the quotation is standing on top of. Müller’s 1881 English, and worth reading slowly: it says what we are follows from what we have thought, and then immediately makes that concrete and moral — act from an evil thought and pain follows you. It is not telling you to think yourself into being someone else.

source.rightsNote: The excerpt above is safe to reuse: Müller’s 1881 translation is long out of copyright everywhere, which is exactly why we quote him rather than a modern translator whose text would still be protected. The quotation on this page is a different matter — it is modern prose of unestablished authorship, so there is no clean public-domain claim to make about it. Quote the Dhammapada freely; quote the maxim as an anonymous modern saying. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Gautama Buddha
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on the Buddha
author.metaLine: c. 5th century BCE · founder of Buddhism · northern India
author.bio: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught in northern India around the fifth century BCE. The Dhammapada — the one Buddhist book most Western readers have actually opened — opens with two verses about mind and thought, and that opening is why this particular maxim finds him so easily: it sounds like a compressed version of a page people vaguely remember. The compression is where the meaning changes. The Buddha is describing how action rooted in a state of mind carries consequences; the maxim promises that thinking about a self will produce one.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Most misattributions have one false owner. This one has two, and the pair is the interesting part: when a line bounces between the Buddha and Gandhi, that is usually a sign it belongs to neither and is being assigned by vibe.

items.why: Not in the Dhammapada, not in the Nikayas, in no wording. The nearest genuine passages — Dhammapada 1–2 and Majjhima Nikaya 19 — are about karma and mental habit, not about becoming what you picture the trace ↗.

What circulates under Gandhi’s name is ‘A man is but the product of his thoughts. What he thinks, he becomes’ — carried in anthologies of his writing rather than traced by us to a dated original, and in any case not the wording on this page. People then shorten it, and the shortened form drifts back to the Buddha. Two famous men, one floating sentence.

items.who: Buddha for Gandhi, Gandhi for Buddha
items.why: The credit swaps depending on the venue: meditation and mindfulness contexts hand it to the Buddha, political and self-improvement contexts hand it to Gandhi. Neither ever produces a page number, which is the tell.

If the 1897 trace holds, the sentence comes out of American New Thought — the movement that runs from Trine through Think and Grow Rich to The Secret. That is a philosophy of mind creating circumstance, which is close to the opposite of a teaching built on non-self and letting go.

misattribution.truthLine: Neither man. No canonical source, no dated Gandhi original for this wording, and an earliest documented English instance in an 1897 New Thought bestseller the trace ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Six words of promise: whatever you are is up to you, starting now. It is the most portable self-help sentence ever written, which is why it works equally well on a gym wall, a startup deck and a meditation app, and why nobody stops to ask where it came from.

The double attribution is doing real work. Attach it to the Buddha and it reads as ancient wisdom; attach it to Gandhi and it reads as proven in practice. Either name converts a motivational slogan into an authority, and the slogan is identical underneath.
context.detailsSummary: The Dhammapada version, and why it is not the same
detailsBody: Dhammapada 1 (Müller, 1881): what we are results from what we have thought — and acting from an evil thought brings pain after it, like the cart-wheel following the ox.
Dhammapada 2 is its twin: act from a pure thought and happiness follows like a shadow that never leaves.
That is a causal claim about conduct and consequence. It is not a claim that visualising an outcome produces it.
Majjhima Nikaya 19 makes the psychological version: what you keep thinking about becomes the direction your mind leans. True, modest, and not the same promise.
The gap between those and 'what you think you become' is the whole reason this page exists.
context.pull: When a line bounces between the Buddha and Gandhi, it usually belongs to neither.
